display_title: Interesting problem but methodological contribution and experimental evaluation not compelling

content.title: Interesting problem but methodological contribution and experimental evaluation not compelling
content.review:
The paper is about overcoming the limitation of current conditional generative imaging approaches to learning from data where only a single output image is available for a single conditioning. The paper builds upon IMLE [Li & Malik 2018] and [Li et al 2020]. In particular, the current approach seems to expand [Li et al 2020] with a mapping network. The benefits of the architecture are highlighted on two tasks: image super-resolution and image decompression. 

Pros:
-> the paper deals with a very interesting subject of interest to the ICLR community
-> the reported results show superiority of the model over [Li et al 2020]


Cons:
-> the paper's presentation could be improved, from the current version it is unclear what are the contributions of the work ,and the connection with Li et al 2020 are not explicitly discussed
-> the model modification seem to be incremental
-> there are some details missing in the experimental evaluation (e.g. number of trainable parameters).


Detailed review and clarification question:

Presentation: 
 - The paper very heavily borrows from Li et al 2020 and this is not properly acknowledged in the current presentation of the paper. I would encourage the authors to rewrite the paper highlighting the connections and the differences with Li et al 2020 more explicitly. 
- From the current paper presentation, it is unclear what are the paper contributions. Based on my reading of the paper, it seems that the main paper contribution is in the model. However, stating the contributions clearly in the introduction and splitting the Methodology into "Methodology" (modifications w.r.t. prior approaches) and "Background" (overview of related works such as Li et al 20202 and Li & Malik 2018) would ease the understanding of the paper. 

Choice of tasks:
- Why did authors decide to tackle these particular two tasks (super-resolution and decompression)? Why not include image synthesis from segmentation masks as in Li et al 2020?

Method:
- There seem to be two changes in the model w.r.t. Li et al 2020: the second branch (mapping network) and weight normalization. Adding some explanation on why these design choices are beneficial for the task would make the methodological section stronger.
- "Regression models take the form of a deterministic function from x to y, and so p(yjx) is always a delta". I think that this sentence is not 100% exact. This would depend on the formulation of the regression model, e.g. one could regress a Gaussian distribution and fit he model with gaussian log likelihood.

Evaluation metric:
- In general, I'm not convinced if FID is the right metric for the task. Could the authors motivate the use of FID metric? What is the effect of ImageNet pre-trained inception model on the metric values? Moreover, could the authors clarify what is the reference distribution used to calculate FID?

Experimental evaluation:
- Could the authors add the numbers of parameters next to each model? How many additional parameters does the introduced model have when compared to Li et al 2020? Could the authors comment on whether the observed improvements could be attributed to the potential increase in number of parameters as opposed to the model design choices?

Quantitative results:
- Although embedding videos in the pdf is a nice thing to do. It would also be beneficial to see images and difference maps in the main body of the paper. The embedded videos require Acrobat Reader software.

The paper lacks discussion on the method's limitations. Could the authors comment on the potential limitations of the proposed approach?


Overall, I recognize the importance of the task that is being tackled in the paper. However, I find the presentation of the paper to be rather misleading (acknowledging the similarities/differences with Li et al. 2020 would be beneficial), the importance of methodological contributions to be unclear, and the experimental evaluation not fully compelling.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Key Contributions and Other Clarifications
content.comment:
The similarities with Li et al. 2020 are just that (1) both our paper and Li et al. 2020 use conditional IMLE and (2) both consider some form of super-resolution as one of the tasks. The similarities end there, however. Below are the key high-level contributions of our paper:

(1) We tackle 16x super-resolution, whereas Li et al. 2020 tackles 4x super-resolution. 16x super-resolution is substantially more challenging, as evidenced by the poor performance of leading 4x methods on the 16x task. We compare to Li et al. 2020 (SRIM) in our paper (see figures in the appendix) and our results have much higher visual fidelity. This shows the importance of the technical contributions (detailed below) of this paper. 

(2) Li et al. 2020 uses a different model for each task, whereas we use the same model for three different tasks (16x super-resolution, decompression and recovery of unobserved principal components), demonstrating the generality of the model. 

(3) Li et al. 2020 does not outperform single-output GAN-based methods (which only produce a single output image for each input image) in terms of visual fidelity, and so imposes a tradeoff between visual fidelity and sample diversity. On the other hand, our method outperforms even single-output GAN-based methods (such as ESRGAN) and eliminates this tradeoff. This shows the importance of the technical contributions (detailed below) of this paper. 

(4) The non-SR-based problem considered in Li et al. 2020 is easier than the one tackled in our paper, in the following sense: the problem considered in Li et al. 2020 is that of generating images from segmentation masks - in that problem, the factors of variation across different inputs are the same, i.e. changing weather or time of the day (this was discussed in Sect. 4.3 of Li et al. 2020). On the other hand, the factors of variation for image decompression depend on the content of the input image, making them harder to learn. 


Below are the technical contributions:

(1) Our paper uses a model that progressively upscales an image in multiple stages (where each stage upscales by 2x) as discussed in Sect. 4.1, whereas the model Li et al. 2020 upscales to the final resolution in one go. 

(2) Our model takes noise of varying resolutions as input, and we introduce a hierarchical sampling strategy as discussed in Sect. 4.1. On the other hand, Li et al. 2020 uses the standard conditional IMLE sampling strategy, which generates samples i.i.d. 

(3) Our paper uses intermediate supervision at varying resolutions, whereas Li et al. 2020 does not. 

(4) Our paper adds weight normalization and uses a mapping network. 

As evidenced by the substantial difference in visual fidelity of the results of our method and those of Li et al. 2020 (SRIM), these contributions are important. 

Presenting a new problem setting (generative unobserved alternatives), a relatively new framework (IMLE), a new model (HyperRIM), different tasks (super-resolution, decompression and recovery of unobserved principal components) and the differences from prior IMLE models all within the allotted page limit would be challenging. Unfortunately we had to make sacrifices - we tried to make the paper self-contained by including the essential background on IMLE but had to leave out details that are not essential to understanding the present paper (such as the model used in Li et al. 2020), but hope the above explanation clarified the contributions of our paper relative to Li et al. 2020. 

Choice of Tasks:

As mentioned above, image synthesis from segmentation masks is an easier task because the factors of variation are the same across different input segmentation masks. As a result, the benefits of our method cannot be fully demonstrated using this task. 

Method:

The point of the paper is to show that the proposed architectural additions (mapping network and weight normalization) are broadly useful in IMLE-based models and are not specific to the task. Why the various normalization schemes in deep learning should work at all (even more widely-used ones such as batch normalization) is still an active topic of research in learning theory, so we defer to that literature. 

"Regression models take the form of a deterministic function from x to y, and so p(y|x) is always a delta": when least squares is interpreted as estimating the mean of a Gaussian using maximum likelihood, to generate predictions, we typically use the point estimate of the mean rather than the Gaussian itself. What we mean here is that the point estimate is a delta. 

Evaluation Metric:

FID is used to measure the visual fidelity of a distribution of generated images. We cannot use an evaluation metric that penalizes deviations from the original image because the point of our paper is to generate alternative but plausible output images. It's been empirically shown in various papers that the particular Inception features used by FID correlate well with visual fidelity. 

Continued below...

replying_to: Replying to Key Contributions and Other Clarifications

content.title: Key Contributions and Other Clarifications (cont'd)
content.comment:
...continued from above

The reference distribution is the empirical distribution of original images, so FID measures the visual fidelity of a large pool of image samples generated from all inputs. In other words, it measures the visual fidelity of the marginal distribution over generated images. 

Experimental evaluation:

We tried increasing the number of parameters in Li et al. 2020 so that they take up the same amount of memory as our model, but performance was not much different from the original model proposed in Li et al. 2020. 

Potential limitations:

When applied to a new task, some degree of hyperparameter tuning is needed to achieve the best results. However, this is true with other kinds of deep generative models, and in our experience, hyperparameters are easier to tune for our method than for GAN-based methods because a slight tweak to the hyperparameters in a GAN can cause training to diverge, whereas our method can always train stably.

content.title: This paper is targeting an attractive problem but further experiments are necessary to support the idea
content.review:
This work should target a one-to-many task, which is an interesting topic. However, the study cases, i.e., SR and decompression, do not well demonstrate the claim of "generating unobserved alternatives." Besides, these two cases may be unsuitable examples for generating alternatives since their goals should be identical recovery of the ground truth. For these tasks, the proposed work should be compared to SOTA in PSNR. 

It may be unfair to compare to stacked ESRGAN since it is not trained jointed, while your model is directly optimized towards 16x. It would be better if compare at 4x. Moreover, it is still unfair to compare to standard SR methods using faithfulness-weighted variance because SR methods would avoid randomness in design. And the similar problem for the compression task.

In general, more suitable tasks would make the idea better motivated.

display_title: Re-emphasizing the Point of the Paper

content.title: Re-emphasizing the Point of the Paper
content.comment:
Below is our response to each point raised in the review:

Q1: "these two cases may be unsuitable examples for generating alternatives since their goals should be identical recovery of the ground truth"

A1: As we emphasized in our introduction (paragraph 4), inverse problems such as SR and decompression are *ill-posed*, so the input cannot uniquely determine the output. So goals of SR and decompression should *not* be "identical recovery of the ground truth" because doing so is fundamentally impossible. The central point made in the paper is that there is no sole ground truth, and the original image is just one of many possible output images. 

Q2: "the proposed work should be compared to SOTA in PSNR"

A2: As mentioned in our response to R4, PSNR assumes a unique ground truth and any deviation from the ground truth should be penalized. This is not appropriate for our setting because our goal is to generate *unobserved alternatives*, that is, other images different from the ground truth that are also visually plausible. 

Q3: "do not well demonstrate the claim of 'generating unobserved alternatives.'"

A3: There is no justification for this criticism anywhere in the review. In fact, we do demonstrate the generation of many output images for the same input image in our results (Figs. 6 and 8 for example). This also shown quantitatively by faithfulness-weighted variance, which is higher than the baselines. 

Q4: "It may be unfair to compare to stacked ESRGAN since it is not trained jointed, while your model is directly optimized towards 16x. It would be better if compare at 4x. "

A4: The crux of this criticism seems to be we should not tackle a more challenging problem simply because the state-of-the-art method (ESRGAN) tackled an easier problem. This reasoning does not make sense - if every paper focuses on finding better ways to solve an easy problem, we as a field are doomed to making incremental advances. 

Q5: "It would be better if compare at 4x"

A5: Comparing at 4x doesn't make sense, because that is an easier problem where the input constrains the output to a greater extent. As mentioned in the opening paragraph of Sect. 4, we picked the more challenging 16x setting because "under this setting, the input contains much less information about the output, and so there could be a lot more valid output images for the same input image." Because our goal is to generate unobserved alternatives, 16x is the appropriate problem setting. 

Q6: "It may be unfair to compare to stacked ESRGAN since it is not trained jointed"

A6: We tried joint training, but could not get it to train at all because of the training instability of GANs. 

Q7: "SR methods would avoid randomness in design"

A7: The point of the paper is to generate unobserved alternatives, i.e. many high-res versions of the same low-res image. This is necessary because 16x SR is severely ill-posed. Because it is fundamentally impossible to generate the original image, randomness is an essential component of the method and allows generation of many plausible outputs. Methods that avoid randomness therefore cannot handle the severely ill-posed setting. 

Q8: "And the similar problem for the compression task."

A8: Being able to generative alternative versions of the output is not a bug - it is the whole point of the paper.

replying_to: Replying to Re-emphasizing the Point of the Paper
display_title: Concern on the choice of applications

content.title: Concern on the choice of applications
content.comment:
Thanks to the authors for emphasizing the key points. I understand that the proposed algorithm is to generate something unseen/alternatives. If it is applied to a general image generation task, it is good to evaluate by FID and faithfulness-weighted variance. But for the SR task, it will expect a metric to measure the distance between prediction and ground truth. SR indeed has the ill-posed problem, but the general goal is still to recover something close to the ground truth. The evaluation part mainly focuses on perceptual quality and diversity, but has ignored the fundamental motivation of SR.
Besides, generating alternatives may not be well motivated for the SR task. I think ill-pose is a challenge of SR that need to be solved, rather than a strong motivation for generating alternatives.  

For comparison to 4x ESRGAN, it does not mean to discourage advanced research. The fair comparison should be of central importance when comparing to SOTA. If 16x models are unavailable, comparison at 4x will be necessary. It may not make sense to the proposed method, but it makes sense to SR. If you could also beat SOTA at 4x, the proposed method would be stronger.  

Above all, the main concern is the applications chosen in this paper, which distract the reviewers from the algorithm.

replying_to: Replying to Concern on the choice of applications
display_title: This paper is a method paper rather than an applications paper

content.title: This paper is a method paper rather than an applications paper
content.comment: The point of the paper is to propose a new machine learning method with new capabilities, rather than to beat SOTA on a specific task. To demonstrate those capabilities, we picked 16x super-resolution. We did not pick 4x super-resolution because 4x super-resolution is less ill-posed and so multiple plausible output images may not be available for a single input image. Hence demonstrating results on 4x super-resolution does not substantiate the main claim of the paper, namely that the proposed method can generate unobserved alternatives. In other words, 16x super-resolution is merely used as an example to demonstrate a scenario where multiple valid output images are possible; we could have picked other tasks that have this property and did (e.g.: recovery of unobserved principal components and image decompression) -- and demonstrated results on those tasks too. Whether or not the goal of traditional SR is to recover the original image is beside the point - we defined the goal of the task we consider in our paper and that goal could be different from the goal of traditional SR.

content.title: Generating Unobserved Alternatives: A Case Study through Super-Resolution and Decompression
content.review:
This paper considered a setting where the prediction problem is inherently one-to-many, but where the supervision is only one-to-one. They explored several problems with this characteristic and demonstrated that our approach was able to generate different plausible outputs for the same input, even though only one output per input is available as supervision. Moreover, they introduced an architecture for IMLE which outperformed GAN-based methods and can offer benefits like training stability and the lack of mode collapse.


1.	Lack of more indicators to compare, such as PSNR, SSIM, etc.

2.	As for the division of training set and test set, the experimental visualization result diagram scene is relatively simple and does not compare on the standard datasets such as SET14, Managa109, and its generalization ability remains to be proved.

3.	In addition, the meaning of the tanh+ Offset in Figure 3 is not clearly explained.

4.	Some little spelling mistakes, the word "thee" in the third line from the bottom of page 3 should be changed to "the".

content.title: Problem Setting Requires Different Evaluation Protocols
content.comment:
1. PSNR and SSIM both measure similarity of the generated image to the original image, which inherently assumes that the original image is the sole ground truth that should be considered correct, and any deviations from it should be penalized. This paper challenges this notion - as we pointed out in the introduction, "(1) for the same input, there could be multiple prediction targets that are correct, but (2) only a single prediction target per input is given as supervision". In other words, there is nothing wrong with generating a high-res image different from the original image, as long as it is visually plausible. To measure how visually plausible the results are, we reported FID and faithfulness-weighted variance based on LPIPS, both of which account for perceptual similarity and can handle a distribution of generated high-res images rather than just a single high-res image. 

2. To generate multiple versions of high-res images, one must have seen multiple instances of the same object category, i.e.: different birds for example. Datasets like Set14 or Manga109 do not have different images of the same category and so are not appropriate for our setting. So we used ImageNet which does have many images of the same category. ImageNet is widely considered to be a challenging dataset (see the discussion in BigGAN for example), and we argue that it is more challenging than Manga109 which only contain cartoon images. We clearly demonstrated that our method outperforms leading methods on ImageNet, so even if one were to view ImageNet as "simple", the fact that leading methods don't do well would demonstrate otherwise. 

3. tanh + offset is (tanh(x) + 1)/2, i.e. shifting and scaling tanh so that its range is [0,1]

4. Typos will be fixed.
